children.text: On January 12th, Terrapreta was invited by Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore to present its five-year journey in transforming Nature-based Solutions (NbS) into reality to students on the Master's in Cultural Projects programme. The session explored how complex ecosystem restoration initiatives are built on a foundation of scientific expertise, strategic partnerships, and compelling storytelling.

Drawing on experiences from our pilot project Osservatorio La Goccia—a living laboratory in Milan tackling soil bioremediation and forest restoration—Stefano Zoli highlighted the critical role that collaboration plays in scaling environmental impact. The presentation underscored that successful Nature-based Solutions require more than technical expertise; they demand skilled communicators and coordinators who can mobilize diverse stakeholders and translate scientific complexity into actionable narratives.

For students entering the field of cultural project management, the session demonstrated that environmental restoration and cultural initiatives share a fundamental challenge: turning vision into sustainable, measurable impact through networks of partners.
Terrapreta extends special thanks to Ivana Vilardi for the invitation and facilitation!

children.text: Contemporary territories are highly complex systems, consisting of the overlapping of numerous factors (actors, uses, practices, histories, rules, environmental conditions, infrastructural constraints and available resources). Today, implementing a land transformation project means systematizing this complexity into an effective and innovative strategy, through a new approach to design that is data-driven and can be monitored and evaluated.

Whether it is for a green plan, the redevelopment of an industrial district or the restoration of an ecosystem, qualitative and quantitative data are key assets that need to be collected for a specific area and organised into an accessible dataset, so that they can be easily used by every stakeholder involved in the process to generate greater impact.
Through a step-by-step process, we help public administrations and private landowners to promote and develop innovative processes for long-term land transformation.

Thanks to a multidisciplinary scientific approach and a wide range of activities (iterative field surveys, research and synthesis, censuses, monitoring, specific and experimental analyses), we can “read” and understand a territory or a single site in depth, producing documents and sets of information (Baseline) that frame problems and opportunities, informing planning, design and communication.

Once the Baseline has been defined, we work together with all stakeholders involved in the process to develop a shared vision and a strategy or masterplan for implementing complex and innovative projects.

children.text: Between 5 and 8 October 2025, a workshop took place with adolescents from the CAG “Il Poliedro” youth centre in Villapizzone (Milan), created to explore their relationship with La Goccia Forest.

Twelve students joined activities coordinated by Kilowatt, partner of the Osservatorio La Goccia, together with Caterina Moroni—artist and performer—who guided them into the forest’s unique reality through collective and individual sensory practices.

Day after day, their sense of wonder and curiosity grew—first as a group, and then as active participants in sharing what they were learning. On the final day of the workshop, the teens took on a new role: they led a group of neighbourhood residents on a walk inside the forest, helping turn exploration into community storytelling.

children.text: On July 21, an exhibition was inaugurated in which several entities engaged in reuse architecture and interdisciplinary research participated. Terrapreta displayed a table with materials, books and photos on the soil universe with its dynamics and secrets, with three panels on the history of the Osservatorio La Goccia.

On 13 and 14 September, as the exhibition drew to a close, Terrapreta took part in the roundtable discussion with architecture practices and associations, including AIPAI and Archivio Storico Olivetti.

Surrounded by the sound of the Metauro River in the walls that first housed the Ducal Paper Mills, then the Carotti Wool Mill and today are a virtuous example of hydroelectric power generation, it was also an opportunity to remember Giancarlo De Carlo, who gave so much to the architecture of this area.

children.text: Within Lombardini22’s Impact–Sottocasa project, Terrapreta carried out a soil assessment—together with the Pedology group of DISAT at the University of Milan–Bicocca—on the plot between Via Lombardini and Via Autari, inside Parco Baden Powell (Milan).

The site previously hosted a plant nursery and a paint business and was remediated via excavation and backfilling around ten years ago. Today, the soil is predominantly sandy and shows signs of compaction linked to past machinery traffic, with ash (Fraxinus) and sweetgum (Liquidambar) bordering the area.

We selected six sampling points and combined laboratory and field observations to build a solid picture of current soil conditions. The workflow included circular paper chromatography (Pfeiffer Circular Chromatography), a qualitative method that produces characteristic ring patterns on treated filter paper from soil extracts to support an integrated reading of soil features. We also measured soil penetration resistance with a penetrometer, a standard approach used to gauge how strongly soil resists penetration and to flag potential compaction-related constraints for roots and water movement.

At three sampling points, we described soil colour using the Munsell Soil Color Charts, a widely used reference to standardise soil colour description and support interpretation of moisture-related conditions (including very wet/gleyed soils). All results were consolidated into a technical report with a dual purpose: supporting the urban forestry / Nature-based Solutions design within the Impact project and establishing a baseline for future impact monitoring.​

The collaboration was enriched by the involvement of Open Fabric and forestry expert Dr Roberto Musmeci, and helped refine a preventive soil-diagnosis approach designed to make urban NbS interventions more robust—especially on post-remediation sites where physical soil constraints can strongly shape outcomes.

children.text: To achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, we need to develop climate change adaptation and mitigation strategies that rely on technical solutions that are Nature-based. In this way we can optimize the use of resources, improving wider areas and generating a greater and better impact.

NbS are cost-effective solutions that can be implemented with low budgets and high positive impact in different contexts such as public spaces, urban streets, private properties and commercial sites. They can also help mitigate and offset the environmental impacts of buildings and infrastructure.
With Landscape architecture, we synthesize inputs from different disciplines to give shape to NbS, regenerating places and ecosystems for nature, people and climate.

From small public areas to large-scale projects, we design solutions for contemporary climate challenges through interventions such as reforestation and microforests, soil bioremediation and desealing, ecological and functional connections, rainwater management and nature-based water-management systems.

name: La Goccia Urban Forest

children.text: Le Officine del Gas
and the forest
In 1905 the
Union de Gaz de Paris
built the
Grandi Officine del Gas della Bovisa

on a parcel of land shaped like a falling drop, enclosed on every side by railway tracks. The shape gave the area its name. For half a century the works gasified coal to light Milan. As the technology changed the plant was decommissioned in stages and closed for good in 1994.

The plant's gates then stayed shut for thirty years. Pioneer species arrived first and dropped enough leaf litter to build humus. The new soil brought insects, then animals, then plants long considered lost from the Milanese plain. The site now holds eighteen hectares of forest, roughly fifteen thousand trees, more than 250 vascular plant species and forty species of birds, all of it growing on contaminated ground.

Eighty-five years of gas production contaminated the soil. Thirty years of abandonment grew a forest over it. Our work is to undo the damage the industry left without losing the ecosystem that grew in its place. When it is finished, La Goccia will be one of the largest contaminated sites in Europe restored through Nature-based Solutions, and a park of a kind Milan has not had before.
Reading the forest, 2021

In June 2021 we surveyed the spontaneous vegetation. We wanted a figure for what the forest was worth, because until then it had only ever been counted as a cost. We ran it as a citizen science survey: over five days about forty people catalogued the trees, shrubs and herbaceous species growing on the site.
Using the sample area method with iTree Eco, we produced a biomass account for the whole forest and a first estimate of the ecosystem services it provides.
The report opened the conversation with the City of Milan. It led to the collaboration pact of September 2022, and to the founding of Osservatorio La Goccia.
The Osservatorio
Osservatorio La Goccia

is the partnership we put together to do the work, and have led since. It started in 2022 with the Municipality of Milan, the Natural History Museum of Milan, CNR-IRET, CFU Italia Nostra and Progetto Natura Onlus. For the European project it grew into an ATS and took on soil science, water engineering, microbiology and social research: Università Statale di Milano, Università di Milano-Bicocca, Iridra, M3R, Kilowatt, cheFare, Futurecologies and PACT.

The forest is already doing part of the clean-up. To help those processes along we had to understand them in detail, so what followed was baseline work: a preparatory analysis plan, a strategic direction document, a supplementary soil characterisation campaign, a full forest census, fauna monitoring, forest soil analysis, and an assessment of how far the ecosystem can recover on its own. The work continued under the 2022 pact, then PNRR funding, and now the European grant.
More information at: osservatorio-goccia.org
GOCCIA, European Urban Initiative

Since December 2024 the work has been funded by GOCCIA, Green Opportunities to Clean-up Contaminants through an Interspecies Alliance, a European Urban Initiative Innovative Action financed in part by the ERDF, led by the Municipality of Milan and running to 2028.
Terrapreta leads Osservatorio La Goccia, one of eleven partners in the consortium and the largest after the Municipality.

Through it we lead Work Package 6, Nature-based Solutions for soil and water restoration. We map the soil across the site for fertility, organic matter, carbon storage and water infiltration. We run the experimental desealing plots, lifting asphalt to watch what roots and new topsoil do without help. And we monitor the plant and microorganism systems that determine what the reclamation should do next.

We also lead the project geodatabase. It holds biodiversity, microclimate, soil and water data from every partner in one versioned reference, and feeds the ecological and microclimatic models the project runs on.

The grant also pays for the recovery of a disused warehouse on site, the Ranch, for forest management run with the public, an ethnographic programme, and a governance model that counts the environment itself as a stakeholder.
The project and its programme: eui-goccia.eu
Designing the park

The RPBW masterplan set the frame for the wider area, the Politecnico's Campus Nord, the Fondazione Scuole Civiche and the rebuilt Bovisa and Villapizzone stations, and assigned the public land to the north to the recovery of the forest.

We are a main partner of the Municipality of Milan for the restoration project and a landscape architecture consultant to MM Spa during the design phase. The operational reclamation plan has been approved. The landscape design of the park is in progress and concludes in 2026, with the park delivered by the end of 2028.

Remediation runs area by area, in phases, over several years, combining phytoremediation and other bioremediation methods with desealing and reforestation. The park opens in stages as it goes, rather than all at once at the end.

What opens is not a conventional park. Some areas take visitors. Others stay closed, kept for the species already living there, because the forest is the reason the site is worth recovering at all. In a city facing hotter summers and heavier rainfall, eighteen hectares of mature woodland does work that new planting could not match for decades. La Goccia is being designed to protect that first, and to let Milan in around it.

children.text: Urban soils are often degraded and lack a sufficient degree of health to function properly. This reduces their capacity to generate ecosystem services, in terms of fertility, biodiversity, water retention, capacity to store carbon and to host healthy vegetation.
Through soil analysis and low-tech agronomic interventions we work to restore soil health in areas of all sizes from small roadside beds to large green areas.

Our “pre-planting process” rapidly improves soil quality and creates suitable soil conditions for planting vegetation, helping public administrations, designers and private landowners to improve soil health and reduce plant mortality during plant establishment, achieving forestation goals faster.

name: A2A Garden
shortDescription: At A2A's waste-to-energy plant on the western edge of Milan, we turned a low-diversity lawn into a climate garden. A winding gravel path leads visitors through 2000 square meters of drought-tolerant perennials, grasses and shrubs. A small, resilient ecosystem in the middle of an industrial site.
